newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's new tax laws to raise 30-35 trln rbls.
newsitem.headline: Russia's new tax laws to raise 30-35 trln rbls.

text.p: A package of new tax amendments to be discussed by the State Duma lower house of parliament on Wednesday would raise 30-35 trillion roubles in 1997, Deputy Finance Minister Sergei Shatalov said on Tuesday.

"We are talking about corrections now," Shatalov told a news conference. "The strategic course is to review our approach to tax privileges. There are so many of them that it endangers budget revenues."
The Duma plans to discuss the 1997 draft budget on Friday.

In October, the Duma rejected the 1997 draft budget, criticising it for over-optimistic revenue forecasts and poor provisions for social spending. The government and parliament then set up a reconciliation commission to agree on a new version.
The new version of the 1997 budget sets revenues of 401.97 trillion roubles, and spending of 497.37 trillion, for a deficit of 95.40 trillion, or 3.5 percent of gross domestic product.
Most of the extra revenue, 20 trillion roubles, will come from extending a 15-percent tax on profits from securities to operations with government paper, Shatalov said.
Last month, the Duma rejected a bill to impose taxes on operations with Treasury bills, which have so far been exempt from the tax, but Shatalov said he hoped the laws would be approved by the Duma.
"We are still counting that the Duma will pass the amendments agreed by the concilatory commission," he said. "But statements from some parliamentary groups show this will be difficult."
Other amendments include abolishing tax exemptions on reserve funds set up by joint stock companies, which will bring 1.6 trillion roubles to the budget, Shatalov said.
The government also plans to cut tax privileges on investment, he said.
Companies currently pay only 50 percent of profit tax if the profit is spent on investment and construction. The amendment would restrict this exemption to investment into production, Shatalov said.
Value-added tax exemptions in construction will be limited and in the case of equipment exports, abolished.

The basis for calculating excise on alcohol will shift to a flat rouble charge, adjusted for inflation, reflecting the alcoholic strength of the drink, from a percentage of the sales value. The government plans to use the same approach to imported and domestically-produced alcohol, Shatalov said.
"This will simplify collection of the tax, make control easier, makes tax evasion more difficult and will help setting up similar market conditions for everyone," he said.
The government also plans to introduce a 1.5-percent tax on hard currency purchases by individuals.

The government plans to levy a tax on individuals' bank deposits where rates are higher than the central bank refinancing rate and on profits from credits granted at rates higher than the central bank rate, Shatalov said.

Poor tax collection is one of the most serious economic problems in Russia. The International Monetary Fund has delayed payments of its $10 billion loan to Russia twice over revenues worries but is likely to renew payments this month.
Russia has so far collected more than 70 percent of taxes budgeted for this year and will collect not more than 75 percent by the end of the year, Shatalov said.
He blamed this shortfall on the 1996 budget, which he said had overestimated production growth and underestimated inflation.
--Julie Tolkacheva, Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520
